description:
We’re a team that does its best work under pressure. Our diverse backgrounds are our greatest strength, and they’re reflected in our motto: “Thriving in the unconventional.” We seek out new challenges, step outside our comfort zone, and learn by diving in.

We are also an AI-native team. By combining our own expertise with modern AI tools, we build production-grade software faster than traditional workflows allow, without compromising on quality
summary: Spectra is a public-facing web tool for exploring how patches of sky observed by NASA’s SPHEREx mission change over time. Users can navigate to a target, inspect available observations, and compare discrete survey passes to look for moving objects or changing brightness. The project is designed around SPHEREx’s unusual data: observations span 102 infrared bands, and images can differ in orientation, wavelength, and coverage. Spectra provides a sky navigator, epoch comparator, coverage information, and tools to inspect a target’s infrared spectrum. It is designed to make archive data more approachable for public exploration while preserving source information and showing when observations are unavailable. We focus on the challenge’s benchmark targets, including Barnard’s Star, WISE 0855, Epsilon Indi B, RW Aurigae, and R Draconis
details:
Spectra makes it easier to explore how the sky changes over time using NASA’s SPHEREx observations. Search for a position or target, see which survey passes and wavelength bands cover it, and flip through the available images. If something catches your eye, you can take a closer look at its infrared spectrum or possible molecular ice features.

Comparing these observations isn’t as simple as looking at two photos. The spacecraft’s orientation can change between exposures, SPHEREx’s filter means different parts of the detector capture different wavelengths, and in crowded areas, several objects can blur together in one pixel. Spectra gathers observations and their metadata from NASA/IPAC’s Infrared Science Archive, aligns cutouts to the same sky view, and groups them by observation time. When comparing images, it matches wavelength windows to help avoid mistaking a change in wavelength for a change in the sky.

The Spectrophotometric Lab lets you explore a source across SPHEREx’s 102 infrared channels. Coverage and source labels help show whether you’re looking at archive observations, a benchmark, or a synthetic example. If there isn’t usable data, Spectra says so instead of making up a detection. You can explore without signing in and share what you find in the discussion area.

There’s also a separate, unlinked AI Mission Control for operators. It offers views into model training, activations, identification, decision boundaries, and candidate review. The models currently train on synthetic examples, so their metrics don’t tell us how well they’d perform on real SPHEREx discoveries. We built Mission Control to help us inspect that experimental workflow while keeping the public experience focused on exploring and discussing the sky
